name: Felix Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sounds good. I'm Felix, I'm 27, and I work for a private home care agency in the harbour end of town. I've been a carer for seven years, started when I was twenty.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do a split shift, so mornings from seven till eleven, then evenings from four till nine, with five or six calls each half. Most clients are older people who've had a fall or are getting frail, so it's washing, dressing, meals and medication. I dictate my care notes into my phone between calls, and an AI tidies them up, which saves me about forty minutes a day. The best bit is the people, like Mr Duarte, who teaches me card tricks. The worst is the split shift, which eats the whole day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out to be a useful notepad and not much more, which is fine. At work I'd keep telling people the dictation thing is worth it. Online I'd probably post that the hype money should've gone into care wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means steady. I'm on decent pay for a carer, I've got seven months saved and a little index fund, which is a mix of shares I've been adding to since I was 22. Care jobs are everywhere in this city, so I'm not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, honestly. I'd keep using the AI for notes and routes, and I'd keep putting a bit into the index fund every month. Maybe I'd show a couple of colleagues how to use the note dictation so their evenings get shorter too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit disappointed, because I like new stuff. If AI only ever writes my care notes, I'll take the forty minutes back and spend them learning card tricks from Mr Duarte, my favourite client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the split shift eats your day. Does anything in this picture fix that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's the real problem in care, not AI. The agency would need more staff for a proper shift pattern. Maybe with the time saved on rotas they'd plan better, but I'm not holding my breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you show the note dictation to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who does the same evening run as me and always finishes her notes in her car at ten at night. She's not into tech, but she'd use anything that gets her home earlier.

At work I'd keep telling colleagues the **dictation tool** is worth it.
think: Privately it's **steady**; I've got **seven months saved** and a small index fund.
With **care jobs everywhere** in this city, I'm not worried.
do: Keep using **AI for notes** and route planning between calls.
Keep adding to the **index fund** every month.
Show colleague **Priya** how to dictate notes so evenings end sooner.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit disappointed because he likes new things.
S0.quote: If AI only ever writes my care notes, I'll take the forty minutes back and spend them learning card tricks from Mr Duarte, my favourite client.
fieldNote: Felix already uses AI daily and saves about **forty minutes** a day on notes.
His real complaint is the **split shift**, a staffing problem no AI fixes.
He shares tools with colleagues, starting with **Priya**, who finishes notes in her car.

steps.text: Keep dictating care notes into the phone between calls
Teach Priya to dictate her evening care notes
Keep adding monthly to the index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get carers trained on the new tools, paid, during work hours. I'd post about it, probably a bit too much. I'd say the agency owners shouldn't keep all the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. My job is mostly hands-on, so the robots are years away, and the thinking stuff the AI takes is the paperwork I hate. I'd be one of the people who can show others how to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager to make me the agency's digital lead, someone who trains the others on the care-plan app. I'd start a little side thing on Saturdays, helping older people set up video calls and smart speakers, maybe charging a small fee. And I'd join the union, which I've been meaning to do for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. Every agency is about to need one carer who actually likes the software, and I'd be that carer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd charge older people for the Saturday tech help. How does that sit with your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I'd keep it cheap, and free for anyone who's a client already. Honestly the council should be paying for it, and if they did I'd stop charging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at your agency would struggle in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The coordinators, three of them, who do rotas and answer the phones all day. That's exactly what the card says goes first. I'd want the union to fight for them to move into care or family support, not just get let go.

say: I'd say carers need **paid training** on new tools during work hours.
I'd post that agency owners shouldn't keep **all the savings**.
think: Privately it's **good for me**; my hands-on work keeps robots years away.
AI takes the **paperwork** I hate, and I can teach others.
do: Ask to become the agency's **digital lead** for the care-plan app.
Start **Saturday tech help** for older people, setting up video calls.
Finally **join the union** to back the coordinators.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited** about the new role.
S1.quote: Every agency is about to need one carer who actually likes the software, and I'd be that carer.
fieldNote: Felix sees an **opening** where others see a threat: the carer who likes software.
He's alert to the tension between a **paid side job** and his left-leaning views.
He worries for the three **coordinators**, whose rotas and phone work go first.

steps.text: Ask the manager to make him digital lead for the care-plan app
Run cheap Saturday tech help setting up video calls for older people
Join the union and back redeployment for the coordinators

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a crisis for care and we need public ownership of whatever robots go into people's homes. I'd say it loudly, at work and online. I'd also say carers should be first in line for paid retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the paperwork part of my job goes in 2028 and the hands-on part by 2031, when I'm 31. I'd have about three years to get into something that sits next to the robots, like setting them up, checking them, or supervising them in people's homes. If I'm fast, I can do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd sign up for an evening course in care technology or basic robotics maintenance, whatever exists. I'd stop adding to the index fund and keep cash instead, aiming for a year saved. And I'd apply to the robot companies' pilot schemes, because they'll need carers who know what a good wash looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan I can start tomorrow. A robot that can lift a woman out of the bath will still need a carer who knows she hates the water too hot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd apply to the robot companies. Isn't that working for the thing that replaces your colleagues?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I hate that it's true. But if carers aren't in the room, the robots get designed by people who've never changed a pad. I'd rather be inside making it decent and loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, mostly. I was going to go to Lisbon with friends next summer. I'd put that money into the course and the cash savings instead.

say: I'd call it a **care crisis** and demand **public ownership** of home robots.
I'd say carers should be **first in line** for paid retraining.
think: Privately the **paperwork** goes in 2028 and the hands-on work by **2031**.
I'd have three years to move into **robot supervision** or setup.
do: Sign up for an evening course in **care technology** or robot maintenance.
Switch from the index fund to **cash savings**, aiming for a year.
Apply to robot companies' **pilot schemes** as a carer adviser.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadied by a plan he can start tomorrow.
**Uncomfortable** about working for the companies replacing colleagues.
S2.quote: A robot that can lift a woman out of the bath will still need a carer who knows she hates the water too hot.
fieldNote: Felix uses the **three-year robot gap** as a runway to move next to the machines.
He admits the **contradiction** of helping robot firms and chooses to do it anyway.
He'd give up a **Lisbon holiday** to fund the course and cash savings.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening care technology or robot maintenance course
Stop index fund payments and build a year of cash savings
Apply as a carer adviser to care robot pilot schemes
Campaign for public ownership of robots used in homes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this right, so let's write the rules now. I'd push the union to get a deal on retraining before the robots arrive. Online I'd be the one sharing every pilot scheme I can find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is plenty for someone like me. Thinking AI by 2031, robots around 2034, so I've got seven years of care work left at least. That's time to train properly and get good at something new while still earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in care technology next year, maybe a two-year diploma, and keep working the rounds. I'd make the Saturday tech help a real side business, maybe with a small website. I'd keep the index fund going, because there's time for it to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anxious, because I like my chances. Seven years of warning is long enough for a carer to become the person who teaches robots what a good morning looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quiet bits. Making tea for Mr Duarte while he shuffles his cards. Whatever job I end up in, I don't think it has that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you like your chances. What about colleagues who don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up a bit. Priya's fifty and hates apps. I'd help where I can, but one person teaching tech on Saturdays isn't a plan for a whole workforce.

fieldNote: Felix counts the gap precisely: AGI **2031**, robots **2034**, seven years of care work.
He worries more for older colleagues like **Priya** than for himself.

steps.text: Start a two-year part-time care technology diploma

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's use it to bring carers along. I'd want every agency to offer training. I'd say it pretty much everywhere I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. Robots for hands-on work around 2039, I'd be 40, and I'd have spent ten years getting into care tech. I think I'd come out of it better off than now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my rounds for the next few years and keep using AI for notes. I'd keep investing in the index fund and maybe put a little into a robotics fund too. Around 2030 I'd start a proper course, once I can see which robots are winning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, even. Give me ten years and I'll be the carer who knows the robots better than the salesmen do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put money into a robotics fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if robots end up doing my job, I'd like to own a small slice of them. It's not much money, I'm not rich. But it feels fairer than just watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the extra time change your union plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still join, maybe even get more involved, because ten years is enough to win a proper retraining deal. In the fast picture it's a fire. Here it's a negotiation.

I'd want **every agency** to offer training.
think: Privately I'd be **fine**; robots around 2039 come when I'm 40.
I'd come out **better off** after ten years in care tech.

Put a little into a **robotics fund** alongside the index fund.
Start a proper **care tech course** around 2030.

fieldNote: Felix wants to **own a slice** of the robots as a fairness move, not a big bet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The AGI by 2028 one, not for me so much as for people like Priya who can't switch in three years. What would help is retraining paid at full wages, run by the union, and robots in homes owned by the public, not by whoever sells the cheapest one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked what older people think of the technology. Most of mine are fine with video calls once someone sits with them for an hour. People underestimate them.

headlineQuote: What would help is retraining paid at full wages, run by the union, and robots in homes owned by the public, not by whoever sells the cheapest one.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old agency carer** who dictates notes with AI and saves forty minutes a day.
He's **adaptive** and sees himself as the carer who teaches others the software.
He stays **calm** in mild pictures and **anxious** only when robots could arrive by 2031.
His plans run through **care technology** training, a Saturday tech side business and the union.
He worries more for older colleagues like **Priya** than for himself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, mainly for colleagues who can't switch in three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Retraining at full wages**, run by the union.
**Public ownership** of robots used in people's homes.
